<reason>B built the stronger path under the motion's actual standards. The bar was "meaningfully reduce" and no "large increases" — middling thresholds that B met with state-mandate evidence, a coherent national mechanism, and the decisive escape-valve flip: A's own relocation concession became the case for nationwide coverage. A argued cleverly — dissolving B's contradiction charge via evasion and shortages occurring "in different places," exposing the pre-hire audit blind spot, and the sharp closing point that national coverage removes both the workers' escape valve and employers' cross-state recruitment valve. But A's case was ultimately that B's combination was unproven, while A's own harms stayed unquantified and admittedly unevidenced ("a warning, not clean proof"; no causal estimate on discrimination). B directly answered both pressure questions with real mechanisms (population decline indicating departure, not off-the-books substitution; motive-shrinkage from ~98% instant confirmation), whereas A answered B's questions mostly with honest concessions plus reframes. B's flaws — the "effectively conceded" overclaim and the chronologically impossible "silence on both" jab before A could answer — were real but minor. Against a modest-threshold motion, a demonstrated mechanism beats unmeasured hypotheticals.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's escape-valve flip (B2.1, cashed out in B4.1–B4.2): A conceded state mandates shrank unauthorized populations and attributed it to interstate relocation, and B converted that into the core argument for a national mandate — the valve exists only because coverage is patchwork. A never fully escaped it; A's counters (off-the-books substitution, departure ≠ cessation of US work) were answered by the formal-sector closure logic and went unattached to any magnitude. A's best counter-move — A2.2's "different places" dissolution of B's contradiction charge — was strong but only restored A's critique rather than establishing large harms.</best_rebuttal>
